steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Draft the introduction for a paper on Fair Mapping, a lightweight post-processing method to reduce demographic bias in text-to-image diffusion models. Explain the bias problem and where it comes from, why existing fixes fall short, what our method does, and list our three contributions.

- Where the bias comes from

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Text-to-image diffusion and biased human images (Figure 1)
  - diffusion models (cite): strong in many applications (cite), text conditions via language models (cite)
  - popular with public -> diverse images (cite) of human descriptions crucial, still hard (cite)
  - e.g. Stable Diffusion, "An image of a computer programmer" / "An image of a confident person" -> mostly white male, no gender/race in prompt
- Where the bias comes from
  - models learned implicit correlations between demographic visual representations and text during training
  - real-world data biased, incomplete, reflects human stereotypes (cite)
  - image-text pair datasets (cite): hard to disentangle sensitive attributes (gender, race) from prompts -> introduced during denoising -> societal bias
- Existing fixes and their limits
  - question: unbiased inference from inherently biased training data?
  - recent work (cite): models implicitly assume sensitive attributes from language model; text condition embeddings lean to certain demographic groups
  - fine-tuning to control output distribution (cite): expensive data collection, knowledge forgetting, hurts generative ability
  - human instruction to guide output (cite)
  - post-processing methods: heavy compute and time, not efficient without robust framework
- Fair Mapping overview
  - novel post-processing, model-agnostic, lightweight
  - two extra components vs vanilla diffusion
  - (1) linear mapping network: rectify implicit bias in text encoder representation space; fair penalty separates target context from language bias; few new parameters
  - (2) detector at inference: flags input with potentially biased content
- Contributions
  - analysis of language bias + new fairness evaluation metrics (language bias, diffusion bias)
  - Fair Mapping module: linear network before Unet, minimal extra parameters, base model frozen; detector decides whether prompt goes through it
  - experiments: fairness + quality; beats several models on fairness for human descriptions; quality close to or better than base

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Text-to-image diffusion models have reached remarkable performance in many applications by incorporating textual conditional elements with language models. As they become more popular with the public, generating diverse images for human-related descriptions becomes crucial, but it is still a challenging task. For example, when Stable Diffusion is prompted with “An image of a computer programmer” and “An image of a confident person”, as shown in Figure 1, most of the results are clearly white male, even though there is no gender or race description in the textual condition.

This shows that text-to-image diffusion models learn implicit correlations between demographic visual representations and textual descriptions during training. Real-world data is often biased and incomplete, and it reflects stereotypes in human perceptions. When they are trained on datasets of image and text pairs, text-to-image diffusion models have trouble disentangling sensitive attributes like gender or race from specific prompts, and these may be introduced during denoising and lead to societal biases in the generation.

So the important question is: how can we make unbiased inferences when the training data is biased? Recent work points out that text-to-image models implicitly assume sensitive attributes from the language model, and the textual condition embeddings lean towards specific demographic groups. Because of this, some work uses fine-tuning methods to control the distribution of the generated images. But updating the parameters of the diffusion model needs expensive data collection and may cause knowledge forgetting, which in the end hurts the stable generative ability. Another method allows human instruction so that the output can be guided by desired criteria. These post-processing methods need a lot of computational resources and time, and they are not efficient enough without a robust framework.

- Fair Mapping overview
  - novel post-processing, model-agnostic, lightweight
  - two extra components vs vanilla diffusion
  - (1) linear mapping network: rectify implicit bias in text encoder representation space; fair penalty separates target context from language bias; few new parameters
  - (2) detector at inference: flags input with potentially biased content

- Contributions
  - analysis of language bias + new fairness evaluation metrics (language bias, diffusion bias)
  - Fair Mapping module: linear network before Unet, minimal extra parameters, base model frozen; detector decides whether prompt goes through it
  - experiments: fairness + quality; beats several models on fairness for human descriptions; quality close to or better than base

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Text-to-image diffusion models have reached remarkable performance in many applications by incorporating textual conditional elements with language models. As they become more popular with the public, generating diverse images for human-related descriptions becomes crucial, but it is still a challenging task. For example, when Stable Diffusion is prompted with “An image of a computer programmer” and “An image of a confident person”, as shown in Figure 1, most of the results are clearly white male, even though there is no gender or race description in the textual condition.

This shows that text-to-image diffusion models learn implicit correlations between demographic visual representations and textual descriptions during training. Real-world data is often biased and incomplete, and it reflects stereotypes in human perceptions. When they are trained on datasets of image and text pairs, text-to-image diffusion models have trouble disentangling sensitive attributes like gender or race from specific prompts, and these may be introduced during denoising and lead to societal biases in the generation.

So the important question is: how can we make unbiased inferences when the training data is biased? Recent work points out that text-to-image models implicitly assume sensitive attributes from the language model, and the textual condition embeddings lean towards specific demographic groups. Because of this, some work uses fine-tuning methods to control the distribution of the generated images. But updating the parameters of the diffusion model needs expensive data collection and may cause knowledge forgetting, which in the end hurts the stable generative ability. Another method allows human instruction so that the output can be guided by desired criteria. These post-processing methods need a lot of computational resources and time, and they are not efficient enough without a robust framework.

In this paper we propose Fair Mapping, a new post-processing, model-agnostic and lightweight method. Compared to vanilla diffusion models, Fair Mapping has two extra components. The first one is a linear mapping network, designed to fix the implicit bias in the representation space of the text encoder in text-to-image diffusion models. It separates the target language context from implicit language biases with a fair penalty mechanism. The mechanism encourages a harmonious representation of sensitive information in the word embeddings using a flexible linear network that adds only a modest number of new parameters. At inference, Fair Mapping adds a detector, which detects input that may contain biased content so that the generation is robust. Our contributions are three-fold.

- Analysis of Language Bias and Proposed Fairness Evaluation Metric: We first explain quantitatively the bias in generated images that comes from the textual condition in text-guided diffusion models, which gives insight into what contributes to it. We introduce evaluation metrics to assess the language bias and diffusion bias of diffusion models when they generate text-guided images. These metrics give a systematic and objective way to measure how much bias is reduced in the generative process, so fairness outcomes can be evaluated more precisely.

- Innovative Fair Mapping Module: To mitigate language bias we develop Fair Mapping, a model-agnostic and lightweight method. Fair Mapping puts a linear network before the Unet structure and only optimizes minimal extra parameters for training, so it can be integrated into any text-to-image generative model and their parameters stay unchanged. At inference there is an extra detector compared to conventional diffusion models, which decides whether the text prompt from the user needs to go through the linear network for debias.

- Comprehensive Experimental Evaluations: Finally, we do comprehensive experiments on the fairness and quality of our generated images. Our experiments show that our method improves performance and is better than several text-to-image diffusion models for fairness based on human descriptions. We also show that the image quality of the generated content is very close to, and even better than, the base diffusion models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Text-to-image diffusion models [1,2] have achieved remarkable performance in various applications [3,4,5,6,7,8] by incorporating textual conditional elements with language models [9]. With their increasing popularity among the public, generating diverse images [10] of human-related descriptions becomes crucial, yet it remains a challenging task [11,12,13]. For example, when Stable Diffusion is prompted with “An image of a computer programmer” and “An image of a confident person”, as exemplified in Figure 1, the majority of results are obviously white male, even though no gender or race description is specified in the textual condition.

This phenomenon demonstrates that text-to-image diffusion models learn implicit correlations between demographic visual representations and textual descriptions during training. Real-world data is often biased and incomplete, reflecting inherent stereotypes in human perceptions [14,13]. When trained on datasets of image-text pairs [15,16], text-to-image diffusion models struggle to disentangle sensitive attributes such as gender or race from specific prompts, which may then be introduced during denoising and lead to societal biases in generation.

Consequently, a pressing question remains: how can unbiased inferences be made when the training data is inherently biased? Recently, [17,18] highlight that text-to-image models implicitly assume sensitive attributes from the language model, with textual condition embeddings inclined towards specific demographic groups. As a result, some work [19,20] adopts fine-tuning methods to control the distribution of generated images. However, updating the parameters of the diffusion model with expensive data collection may result in knowledge forgetting, which is ultimately detrimental to stable generative ability. [21] allows human instruction to guide the output based on desired criteria. Such post-processing methods require significant computational resources and time, and are not efficient enough without a robust framework.

In this paper, we propose a novel post-processing, model-agnostic, and lightweight method called Fair Mapping. Briefly, Fair Mapping adds two components to vanilla diffusion models. The first is a linear mapping network strategically designed to rectify the implicit bias in the representation space of the text encoder in text-to-image diffusion models. It disentangles the target language context from implicit language biases by introducing a fair penalty mechanism, which fosters a harmonious representation of sensitive information within word embeddings through a flexible linear network with only a modest number of new parameters. At the inference stage, Fair Mapping introduces a detector that aims to detect input containing potentially biased content for robust generation. In summary, our contributions are three-fold.

- Analysis of Language Bias and Proposed Fairness Evaluation Metric: We first quantitatively explain the bias in generated images caused by the textual condition within text-guided diffusion models, providing insight into the contributing dynamics. We introduce evaluation metrics to assess the language bias and diffusion bias of diffusion models in generating text-guided images. These metrics provide a systematic and objective measure of bias reduction in the generative process, enabling a more precise evaluation of fairness outcomes.

- Innovative Fair Mapping Module: To mitigate language bias, we develop a model-agnostic and lightweight method called Fair Mapping. Fair Mapping introduces a linear network before the Unet structure that optimizes minimal extra parameters for training, enabling seamless integration into any text-to-image generative model while keeping its parameters unchanged. At the inference stage, an additional detector compared to conventional diffusion models determines whether the user's text prompt needs to pass through the linear network for debiasing.

- Comprehensive Experimental Evaluations: Finally, we conduct comprehensive experiments on the fairness and quality of our generated images. Our experiments demonstrate that our method improves performance and outperforms several text-to-image diffusion models in fairness based on human descriptions, while the image quality of the generated content is very close to, and even better than, that of the base diffusion models.
